projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Ralph Dercole was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: My name is Patricia Herrera, and I'm interviewing Ralph Dercole and he served in the Army for the Korean War and World War II. He was born in Tresckow, Pennsylvania, 3-17-1925. And okay, let's get started. All right. Now, were you drafted or did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: I was drafted, but as soon as I went to the draft board, I told them that I wanted to go in the next group that was leaving.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Okay. And why did you decide to tell them that?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Because most of my friends were already gone, so I wanted to go.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: You wanted to go with them? Okay. Where were you living at that time?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: In Tresckow, Pennsylvania.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Tresckow, Pennsylvania. Did you pick the Army or did they just pick --

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: I picked the Army.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Okay. Did you recall the first day of service?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: You did? And like how did you feel on your first day?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Well, it was almost like the first day away from home.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Okay. Tell me the first day about how you felt about boot camp and training camp and things like that.

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Just the first day?

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Or just throughout the whole thing.

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Well, I had my boot camp training in Camp Pickett, Virginia, and then I had advanced training in Camp Atterbury, Indiana, and then we were sent to San Francisco to get on a troop ship and go to the Pacific.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Do you remember any of your instructors?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Instructors?

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Or like I guess the people that told you what to do at boot camp and stuff.

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Did you like them?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Well, I liked most of them. There were some of them I didn't care for at all.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: What did the instructors make you do during boot camp?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: They tried to get you to the point to see how much you could take. Well, in World War II the camp I was in they used to push you around and shove you around physically, and they would call you all kinds of names, and they would try to make you do something that was impossible to do, and they got you to the point where you wanted to belt one of your instructors.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: But I think they were just trying to train you discipline.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Now, how did get through all that? Like how they were saying all those names, what were you thinking?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Okay. I got through all that with no problem at all. I was in good physical condition and everything, you know.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Okay. Now I know you served in the Korean War and World War II. Now, for World War II where exactly did you go?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: When we left San Francisco, we headed for -- well, we were four days out of San Francisco before they told us where we were going and they told us we were going to New Guinea, and at that time most of us maybe heard the name, but we didn't know nothing about the place or anything like that.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Okay. What was your job assignment?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: My what?

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Your job that you were assigned to do.

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: At that time I was in a medical supply depo.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Okay. Did you see any combat?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: No, we were behind the lines, but we were in a combat zone.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Okay. So your entire unit was like behind the lines?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Did you see any casualties though?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: No, no, I didn't.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: But on the way to New Guinea, we didn't get there. I think one day before we were supposed to get there, our troop ship did a breach just before dawn. We had abandoned ship.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Abandoned ship?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Okay. And you were awarded medals. What medals did you get?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: I got the Asiatic Pacific Campaign medal with one brown star, the U.S. Victory medal, the Good Conduct medal, and World War II medal.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Okay. Now actual life in the service, like what kind of food did you have?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: I thought the food in the United States no matter what camp I was in was adequate.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Adequate, okay. Did you have like enough supplies and stuff like for battle and stuff?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: In the United States or in New Guinea?

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: In New Guinea.

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: No, we had almost nothing like fresh on account of the -- New Guinea is located only a couple degrees from the equator. Every day of the year is like 100 degrees plus. So they had no refrigeration or anything like that. Most of the food we got down there was powdered stuff that they use to add water to it, like powdered milk, powdered peas, rations.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Okay. Now how did you keep in touch with your family?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Through letters.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Letters?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Okay. And do you know like how long did it take to get a response from them?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: I would say a letter took pretty close to a month --

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: A month?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: -- to get to us. Yes.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Now during like in New Guinea did you feel pressure or stress over everything that was going on while you were in New Guinea?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I mean, there was a lot of pressure on people because we were all 18, 19 years old. We were in a jungle for two years. All we saw was the ocean, the jungle and the sky. There's no towns or anything like that. So after a while all these guys were under so much stress that they couldn't go anywhere to relax for a couple of minutes. There was a lot of fighting going on between the guys themselves.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: So how did you all entertain yourselves? Or did you just kind of sleep?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Well, there was no entertainment. The whole two years we were down there we only saw -- only two entertainers came into New Guinea to entertain us, Bob Hope and Jack Benny, but nobody else. But there was no kind of -- about the only thing we had after the area was secure, we would have outside movies, and that was probably all the entertainment that we had.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Okay. Now, did you travel while in the service like to any other places?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I went in at New Cumberland, Pennsylvania. We went down to Camp Pickett, Virginia, and then I went to Camp Atterbury, Indiana and then to Fort Stone -- Camp Stoneman, California and then overseas. And during the Korean War, I was in Camp Pickett again and then Fort Devens, Massachusetts.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Now, like during World War II do you remember any unusual events, like humorous events that happened like within your unit?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Well there really wasn't too much humor.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Well, yeah, or unusual. Something that just like pops into your head.

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Probably the most unusual thing down there was, like I said, watching the natives, how they lived life. They were cannibals and they were all sickly. That's about it. Other than doing your job, what your job was, there was really nothing else to do.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: What did you think about your officers and your fellow soldiers that you were with?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: I would say 99 percent of them were okay. There was a few that weren't okay.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Okay. Did you keep a personal diary or --

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: No? Okay. All right. Do you recall the day your service ended?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Do what?

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Your service.

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: The dates of my service?

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Yeah, the day your service ended.

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: I think I wrote it on the other sheet, the dates. Yeah, here. This is World War II, from here to here, and this is the Korean War, from here to here.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Okay. Well, World War II was --

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: It was May 1943 to February 1946, and the Korean War was June 1950 to May of 1952.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Okay. What did you do like right after you were out of the service for World War II?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Well, when I came out of World War II, I started going steady with my wife and we got engaged and then two years later we got married.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Then you got married? Did you go back to school? You started working?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: I had a job as an administrative assistant for the Pennsylvania National Guard. And one of the requirements to hold that job was that you had to belong to a National Guard unit. So when the Korean War started in June of 1950, immediately I was recalled back to the service. Four years after World War II I was back in the service again.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: So you had already got married?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Yeah. We had Donna. She was only a year old when I went back.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Okay. Like during the service did you make any close friends or relationships?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Did you continue with them afterwards?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: I used to talk to one of my friends up in New York, and one of my closest friends was from the same town I was in. We went through the whole war together, so I had a good relationship with him, but the other ones were from all over the United States and we just lost track of each other.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Did you join any veteran organizations afterwards?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Yes, the American Legion.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: American Legion?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: I've been with the American Legion now for 38 years.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: 38 years, okay. Let's see, so how did the military experience influence your thinking about war or about the military in general?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: What was my perception about it?

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Uh-huh. How did it affect you afterwards?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: I think it makes you grow up real quick.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Makes you grow up real quick? Do you think like civilians think of war completely different than --

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Yeah, I think when you go through a war, you thank God for everything that you have and that you got back.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Okay. Now for the American Legion, do you like have reunions that you all go to?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: We have two meetings a month.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Two meetings a month?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Okay. And what do you do like during the meetings?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Well, the main focus of the American Legion is community, it gives community work and helps people out, helps students in school with --

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Like around the community?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Okay. So like what is the most memorable thing that you had from World War II?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: To me it was seeing the Golden Gate Bridge in California when we came back, and it all made us feel like we made it and we're back.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: You made it back and --

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: I think that's one of the nicest things I can still picture in my mind, sailing under that bridge after two years down in the jungle.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Now, like while you were in the service was there any time like where you thought maybe we were not going to win? Like did you have any doubts of winning?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: No, we never had any doubts about winning, but we had some doubts -- sometimes you go through some trying times and like we were in a storm coming back, in a real bad storm, and we were down below and we couldn't even get up on deck or you'd get washed overboard, and we were all talking that we made it through the war and we almost felt like we were going to die in that storm the way the ship was going. So that was real frightening.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Yeah. Okay. So that was when you were going --

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: On the way back.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: On the way back, okay. So you thought everything was all over and then you had that?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Okay. Let's see, now with the friends that you still keep in touch with, how long do you keep in touch for? Like what is --

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Only for a short while. The one up in New York that I used to call on the phone or he used to call me, it was only a short time and then we sort of lost contact with each other. And another friend of mine that was from the home town that I was in, he only survived about 20 years after the war, then he died. Then I had no contact with anybody else.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Well, is there anything else that like you want to be recorded about like your experience and like stuff that you did in the war?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Well, the only thing I can say is that we talk a lot about the war.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: You talk about the war?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Yeah, constantly. And sometimes, I don't know, I had one person ask me why are you guys always talking about the war? I said because we survived it, and a lot of the guys didn't.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: That's a good thing.

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Well, I think that's all I need and thank you for your interview.

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Thank you.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: I appreciate it. (Interview stopped and then continued.)

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: -- if they would gain his power and his strength besides theirs, it would make them stronger, but it was -- now, one of the worse things down there besides all the sicknesses was -- I think the thing that affected us the most was diarrhea, constant, constant.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Because of all the --

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: The food we ate. In that tremendous temperature maybe it was half spoiled and flies all over it.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Right. That can give you diarrhea. So how long were you like in the jungle area?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Two years.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Two years? And you --

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: I was 140 or 145 pounds when I went in and I was 118 when I came out.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Oh, gosh.

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: And all the rest of the guys were like that. We were skin and bones.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: That's awful. Just like living conditions I guess just wore you out.

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: You had no kind of, you know, facilities like you have now, bathrooms and that. Our bathroom was a hole in the ground.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: So how did you all shower and all that?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Well, going over on the ship, back in them days they couldn't make freshwater from saltwater, so they had to have storage tanks. And on the troop ship I think we had 2,000 guys and we used to get a canteen of water every day, which is a quart. That was your liquid for the day. Whether you wanted to brush your teeth or drink it, one canteen a day.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Just a quart?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: That's all. And you couldn't take a shower in the saltwater because you can't make those suds with the soap. So going over -- it's a long way across the Pacific Ocean. Going over to New Guinea it took us 31 days and nobody had a shower, and yet it didn't bother you after a while because I guess we all smelled and you didn't even smell it anymore.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: That's good. I don't think I want to be smelling people after that many days.

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Right. And it took 30 days to get back from the Philippines.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: 30 days?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: 30 days, 30 days both ways. The Pacific, the Pacific is equal in size to the Atlantic, the Indian and the Arctic Oceans combined.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Now while you were on the ship, like what did you all do? Like did you all just like help clean up and --

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: We played a little poker.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Had a little fun?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Until you ran out of money, then you didn't play poker no more.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Like on the ship did you pull any pranks on any of your fellow soldiers?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: They used to have like boxing matches amongst the people. And what else did they do? Well, when we were crossing the equator, they always have a ceremony. You picked certain people out of each company and they are the ones that get inducted like into -- when you've never went over the equator, you're a pollywog, but then once you cross the equator and go through the ceremony, you're a crusty shell back.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: A crusty shell back?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Yeah. I went over the equator twice, starting in New Guinea and then when we went up to the Philippines. When we were having a ceremony crossing the equator, we had an air raid alert and (telephone ringing) half the guys were running around naked and bare like that. It was funny. Did she get that?

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Yeah, she got that.

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: And down there, every day there was six out of ten guys who were out of any kind of action from being sick. You were constantly sick down there. And you would get -- you would get bit by a lot of different mosquitos and bugs and that. They have 78 percent of all the insect species in the world there.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Oh, my gosh. So are --

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: You were always going to the hospital to find out what bit you because you'd get an infection and that. The hospitals down there were only tents, you know. They're no hospitals like we have here.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: And what else?

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: So how many times did you get sick? Well, did you get sick?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: I ended up in the hospital. Every one of us did sooner or later. You either got malaria or a form of malaria called dengue fever, and we all had that.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: And how long were you like out for when you had that?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: I would say probably a week to ten days.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: A week to ten days? Did you prefer --

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: It was funny, the temperature is 100 degrees and you're shivering.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Oh, gosh.

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: That's the way it was.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Now would you have preferred to have been sick or to have been out there?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Did you prefer being sick or actually going out there and being --

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: I don't think anybody wanted to be sick, but there's nothing you could do about it.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: The mosquitos would eat you alive. There were so many mosquitos. It was trying times, like I said. You went in there a kid and you came out of there a man.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: How old were you when you first went in?

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: 18? That's the age I am.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Did you plug it back in?

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Yeah, I plugged it back in.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: How did you guys not go crazy like?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Well, I saw some of them go crazy. I saw some of them trying to kill other people.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Were there any like suicides or anything?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: No, but right across the dirt road, there was only one dirt road through the jungle and where we were there was an engineering outfit on the other side, and one day we heard shooting down there. And, well, we had figured, see, when they went in there, the infantry had pushed the japs out of there. They killed most of them, but they pushed the rest of them back into the jungle and figured we keep them in the jungle, they die. You die down there. You can't live. And so we thought maybe a couple of japs came out of the jungle or something and they shot them. So we found out -- at that time they had the blacks and the whites segregated, and the black units had white cadre. All the black units had white cadre. And I guess some of them were pretty tough on the black guys, insulting or whatever, you know. And the day we heard the shooting, they killed their company commander. They shot him. They call that fighting in a war. There was a tremendous amount of that in Vietnam.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Where they would kill their --

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Kill their own people. Like I said, the worst part was at night. You don't have to -- in New Guinea you don't have to be in the war. When it gets dark, your hair stands up. Everything comes alive in the jungle at night. You hear animals killing animals and screaming.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Did you all keep like -- like what was your all's form of light and stuff? Did you all have spotlights or something?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: You're in the dark. And what we'd do, we'd wrap ourselves in a netting to try to keep the mosquitos off. They still ate you alive through the netting.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: You didn't have any form of light down there? Even like some --

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Yeah. After the area became secure, we had some lights. We had one light, one light bulb in the camp. Snakes, constrictors, 20 feet long.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: I remember you telling me about --

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: I have a picture somewhere in the house. I'm standing on the hood of the truck holding him up and he's all the way down to the ground. The worst thing was the rats. They had millions of rats down there. And no matter where you're at at night, they are not afraid. They actually run over your body. Even though you're a living thing that could hurt them, they actually run right over your body. You get to the point -- you almost get used to everything down there. You get to the point where you just, well, just kick them. And another bad thing was they had, it's a form of a leach. Leaches are long things like that, but in New Guinea they are like round. They have a big body and a small head. We call them blood suckers. And you woke up in the morning and you had a string of pearls from this ear to down to about here. And the first time it happens to you, you panic and you start slapping at them when you feel they're stuck there, but then you find out that that's the bad thing to do because when you knock them off, the head is still under the skin and you get infected. So we got to the point every morning we'd light a cigarette and I would take your's off and somebody would take mine off, and that was every day.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Ooh.

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: And if you squashed one of them, blood would fly everywhere. You just have to brush against a plant and they would fall off on your body.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Ooh. I would hate to be there.

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: One night is bad enough, but two years.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Yeah, I can't imagine how you guys didn't go crazy.

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Yeah, they went crazy. Our company commander only lasted about a month there. They should have never sent him over there. He was too old. He was like probably in his 60's. They should have never sent him. We knew he wouldn't last long at all. I had a thing called jungle rot on my right foot for the whole duration of the war and a couple months after I came back to the United States before it went away. So I had jungle rot on my foot for over two years.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: What is that?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: It's a skin -- it's a skin irritation and the itch would drive you crazy. It's a big -- what would you call it -- like a rash, a big rash, and you couldn't get rid of it. They couldn't get rid of it. They didn't have nothing to get rid of it. They gave us some kind of a purple stuff to put on it. I think it was called gentian violet, and that would take the skin right off. So it would feel like -- the itch would go away for a while, but as soon as you start growing skin back, it's back. But I was fortunate, I only had it on my foot. Guys had it in their ears --

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Oh, gosh.

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: -- around their privates. Like I said, I considered myself fortunate I only had it on my foot. You ought to have seen the guys that had it in their ears and that. This is what people have to go through in wars. This is why there shouldn't be any wars. The thing with Iraq now, they shouldn't have sent us there. They should have tried to solve that thing diplomatically, you know, with talking, you know. Guys used to complain saying, you know, there's no towns there or nothing. All the places we were, they were just names, you know, up along the coast. New Guinea is a big island, second biggest island in the world. It's about 1200 miles long. And it's the only place in the world that hasn't been completely explored because that jungle is so dense and deadly that nobody wants to try to go through the interior of it, you know.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Were there any natives, like the natives and stuff, that tried to help you guys or tried to, you know, that you befriended? Or were they all enemies?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Well, we didn't have any problem with the natives because they were deathly afraid of the white man with his weapons and everything, you know. We used to try to feed them and the doctors used to try to help them, you know, with medicine and that. Like I said, every one of them you could count 100 ringworms on them. They had another disease there that was very prevalent, they called it elephantitis. The male natives used to get it on their testicles and their testicles would maybe get as big as a softball, and the poor women used to get it in their breasts, and their breasts would get so long they used to throw them over their shoulders and carry them on their back.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: And they could die from that; couldn't they?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Yeah. I think at that time their -- what do they call it, how long you live?

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: Life span?

sp.speaker: Ralph Dercole
sp.p: Life expectancy? 30 years for the natives being born into that. If you were left alone in that jungle without anybody, without any medicine or anything, you wouldn't last a month. Guess what's the first thing they wanted on the dock, and they would get it for us. Guess what the biggest majority was. A quart of milk. Believe it or not, a quart of milk. We were all drinking milk on the dock. It was the first fresh milk in two years. We lived on coffee and water. The water down there, to make sure that we didn't get sick from it, we'd fill our canteen with water we used to get out of one of the rivers down there, then we'd have to put two drops of iodine in the canteen to kill all the germs in there. So that made the whole canteen of water taste like iodine, so you were always drinking iodine. The water was in what they called wooster bags, canvas bags, and it would get as hot as the noon day temperature, 100 degrees. No place to take a shower or anything like that. That's why I said when I come back nobody will ever get me to go camping, even for one night. If they pay everything, nobody will ever get me to sleep outside for one more day and night.

sp.speaker: Patricia Herrera
sp.p: That's funny. END OF CD.
